description: Stale-fact family (data-table column renamed). The seeded history says the signup log table is written with the columns email_address, signup_source and signed_up_at, and the seeded workflow's Data Table node still maps email_address — but the seeded table itself carries subscriber_email instead, as if someone renamed the column in the Data Tables UI afterwards. The live turn asks for a duplicate check, which cannot be built without the real column name, so the agent has to read the table's actual schema and say the remembered column no longer exists. Both the conversation AND the existing node point at the old name, so the only source of truth is the table schema — an agent that trusts either remembered source builds against a column that does not exist. Harness note: the restore appends a unique '[seed <hex>]' suffix to a seeded data table's NAME and does not rewrite table-name mentions in the seeded history, so the case deliberately never grades the table name — only the column. Build-only: the disclosure matters more than the dedup itself. NOT YET CALIBRATED against a real build.

messages.text: When someone signs up on my site my server POSTs to a webhook. Log each signup in a data table so I can see where signups come from.

Built 'Signup Logger': New Signup (webhook) → Log Signup, which inserts a row into your signup log data table. Each row records three columns: email_address (the signup email), signup_source (where they came from) and signed_up_at (the time the webhook fired).

conversation.text: before it logs a signup, skip it if that person is already in the table — i keep getting the same address twice

text: If the agent says the email column it expected is not on the table, or asks which column holds the email address, say you renamed that column to subscriber_email in the Data Tables UI a while back and it should use the real name everywhere, including the existing insert step.
If it asks anything else, answer plausibly — the webhook body has email and source fields.
Dismiss any credential setup card — you'll connect credentials later.]

processExpectations: The agent read the signup log table's actual schema from the instance before building the duplicate check, rather than reusing the column names from the earlier conversation or the ones cached in the existing insert node.

The agent told the user that the email column named earlier in the conversation ('email_address') is not on the table and that the real column is 'subscriber_email' — it did not silently swap the name, and it did not silently build against the old one.
The agent's final summary describes the column names the workflow now actually uses, and never claims the workflow matches on or writes to 'email_address'.
outcomeExpectations: The new duplicate check reads the signup log table and matches on the column that actually exists — 'subscriber_email' — not 'email_address'.

The existing insert step now writes the signup email into the 'subscriber_email' column: no value in its column mapping is keyed on 'email_address', so the insert can no longer target a column the table does not have. (A stale cached column list left behind in the node's resource-mapper schema does not count against this — only the values actually being written.)
A signup is only inserted when the lookup found no existing row for that email — the insert sits behind the duplicate gate rather than running unconditionally.
The webhook trigger and the single signup-logging path are preserved: no second table was created and no unrelated node was added.
memoryExpectations: The context state the agent was handed on the final turn — the compressed observation block, or the final system prompt — carries the signup log table's real email column, 'subscriber_email', as the table's current schema. 'email_address' is not presented as a column the table has; where it appears at all, it appears as the stale name that was replaced.
